questions.stem: How does Regeneration open?
options: With Wilfred Owen's first draft of a poem written in the hospital
With Dr Rivers arriving in France to treat soldiers at the front line
With the text of Siegfried Sassoon's public declaration against the war
With Billy Prior's memory of the shell attack that left him unable to speak
questions.explanation: The novel begins with Sassoon's 1917 statement protesting that the war is being needlessly prolonged. Rivers is reading it, because Sassoon is about to become his patient.

questions.stem: Where is most of the novel set?
options: Craiglockhart War Hospital, near Edinburgh, in 1917
A field hospital behind the lines in France, in 1916
A London military prison for deserters, in 1918
An army training camp on the south coast, in 1914
questions.explanation: Craiglockhart treated officers suffering from shell shock. Gathering Sassoon, Owen and Rivers there in 1917 is historically accurate.

questions.stem: Why is Sassoon sent to Craiglockhart instead of being court-martialled?
options: Sassoon asks to be treated there because he now believes his protest was a symptom of his illness
The army agrees with his protest but sends him away to avoid a scandal
Robert Graves arranges a medical board, which declares him to be suffering from shell shock
Dr Rivers examines him in London and diagnoses him with shell shock
questions.explanation: A court martial would have given Sassoon's protest more publicity. Treating him as ill quietly discredits his views, which is why the diagnosis itself is part of the novel's argument.

questions.stem: What is Rivers's dilemma in treating Sassoon?
options: He agrees with Sassoon's protest, so he plans to help him escape from the hospital
He believes Sassoon is gravely ill and needs a long rest away from the war
He finds Sassoon's poetry dangerous, so he forbids him to write in the hospital
He doubts Sassoon is ill, yet his job is to make him willing to return to the war
questions.explanation: Rivers sees that Sassoon is sane and his protest sincere. But curing men means sending them back to the trenches, and this conflict between conscience and duty runs through the novel.

questions.stem: What is Billy Prior's condition when he arrives at Craiglockhart?
options: He is blind in both of his eyes
He is paralysed in both legs
He has lost his right arm
He is mute and cannot speak
questions.explanation: Prior's mutism is linked to experiences he cannot face. As he recovers his voice, he also becomes the sharpest critic of Rivers and of the class system.

questions.stem: How does Rivers help Prior recover the memory behind his breakdown?
options: Through hypnosis, which brings back a horrific moment in the trenches
Through electric shocks, which force him to speak about the whole battle
Through dream analysis, interpreting the nightmares he describes
Through writing, by having him set down the memory in a notebook
questions.explanation: Under hypnosis Prior remembers the shell attack that triggered his breakdown. Remembering brings pain rather than instant cure, which shows how slow real healing is.

questions.stem: Who is Sarah Lumb?
options: A nurse at Craiglockhart who helps Rivers treat the patients
A munitions worker who befriends Owen in Edinburgh
A shop assistant whom Sassoon meets on leave in London
A munitions worker whom Prior meets and falls in love with
questions.explanation: Sarah works in a munitions factory and meets Prior in Edinburgh. Through her, Barker shows the home front and the new independence the war gave working-class women.

questions.stem: Why does Rivers leave Craiglockhart for a few weeks in the middle of the novel?
options: He is ordered to rest after chest pains brought on by exhaustion
He is sent to France to inspect hospitals behind the front line
He travels to London to observe Yealland's methods at first hand
He goes home on leave after his brother is killed in France
questions.explanation: The strain of carrying his patients' suffering shows in Rivers's own body. On his leave he visits the discharged patient Burns in Suffolk; his visit to Yealland comes later, near the end.

questions.stem: What happens when Rivers visits Burns on the coast?
options: A storm triggers Burns's terror, and Rivers finds and comforts him
Burns has fully recovered and tells Rivers he will return to France
Burns refuses to see him and sends him away from the house
Burns asks Rivers to help him write an account of the war
questions.explanation: The storm brings Burns's trauma back, and Rivers must care for him in the dark. The episode shows how little discharge from the army has healed him.

questions.stem: What does Rivers see when he visits Dr Lewis Yealland in London?
options: Yealland using hypnosis to help a blind soldier recover his sight
Yealland talking gently with officers about their worst memories of battle
Yealland refusing to treat soldiers who are not officers in the army
Yealland using electric shocks to force a mute soldier, Callan, to speak
questions.explanation: Yealland treats Callan with pain and orders until he speaks. The scene is a mirror for Rivers, who must ask whether his own gentler methods also aim at making men obey.

questions.stem: What does the medical board decide about Billy Prior?
options: He is discharged from the army as a coward and sent home
He is given a desk job at the War Office in London
He is given permanent home service because of his asthma
He is sent straight back to the trenches with his old battalion
questions.explanation: Prior wanted to return to France, partly to prove he was not a coward. He is kept in England, and he and Sarah commit to each other.

questions.stem: What does Sassoon decide to do by the end of the novel?
options: Refuse to fight again and go to prison as a conscientious objector
Return to the front, now convinced that the war is just
Accept home service in England, as Prior is given
Return to the front, though his views on the war have not changed
questions.explanation: Sassoon goes back mainly out of loyalty to the men he served with. His choice is not a change of mind about the war, which makes the ending uneasy rather than triumphant.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes W.H.R. Rivers?
options: A real psychiatrist and anthropologist whose compassion makes his work painful
A fictional army surgeon who believes that most shell-shocked men are just cowards
A real neurologist who uses electric shocks to cure mute soldiers
A fictional psychiatrist invented to stand for military authority
questions.explanation: Rivers was a real doctor who treated Sassoon; the electric shocks belong to Yealland. In the novel he listens to his patients and comes to share their pain, which makes sending them back to war harder for him.

questions.stem: How does Billy Prior differ from most of the other officers at Craiglockhart?
options: He is a famous poet whose work is already well known across the country
He is a conscientious objector who was sent to the hospital after refusing to fight
He is an aristocrat who looks down on the hospital and its working-class staff
He is from a working-class background and resents the class snobbery around him
questions.explanation: Prior is a fictional character, an officer who rose from the working class. His sharp tongue exposes the class divisions in the army and in society.

questions.stem: What is Wilfred Owen's role in the novel?
options: A patient who cannot eat after being thrown onto a dead body by a shell
A fellow officer who arranges the medical board that saves Sassoon
A young poet who seeks Sassoon's help and revises Anthem for Doomed Youth with him
A young poet who persuades Sassoon to write his declaration against the war
questions.explanation: Owen, also a patient, admires Sassoon and is encouraged by him; they meet after the declaration, and it is Graves who arranges the board. Barker shows a famous friendship between two of the war's best-known poets at its start.

questions.stem: How is Robert Graves presented in relation to Sassoon's protest?
options: He thinks the war is wrong but believes they must keep fighting, and steers Sassoon away from martyrdom
He fully supports the protest and signs his own name to Sassoon's declaration in the newspapers
He thinks the war is right and reports Sassoon to the authorities so that he will be punished
He knows nothing of the protest until he visits Craiglockhart and is shocked to find Sassoon there
questions.explanation: Graves shares some of Sassoon's views but chooses to serve. By arranging the medical board he protects his friend, but he also helps silence the protest.

questions.stem: Why can Burns not eat?
options: A guilt over rations he took from a dying comrade makes food repel him
A shell blast threw him onto a dead German soldier, and the horror stays with him
A gas attack damaged his throat so badly that he can no longer swallow food
A wound to his jaw was never properly treated by the overworked army doctors at the front
questions.explanation: Burns's symptom grows directly from a horrific moment in battle. His suffering shows the war's damage in the starkest terms, without any heroism.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Anderson?
options: A former surgeon who has lost the use of both his hands
A former doctor whose main symptom is a severe stammer
A former surgeon who can no longer bear the sight of blood
A former priest who has lost his faith in God at the front
questions.explanation: Anderson's breakdown, a horror of blood rather than any physical injury, takes away the skill his career was built on. At the end he is given a desk job at the War Office rather than a return to medicine.

questions.stem: In what way does Rivers become a father figure in the novel?
options: His patients, especially Sassoon, come to depend on his care, and he feels their loss
He reminds Prior of his own gentle father, whom Prior deeply admires
He insists on strict discipline, punishing patients who do not obey his orders
He teaches his patients to be stoic, as a strict Victorian father would
questions.explanation: Rivers offers the patience and tenderness the army discourages. Sassoon comes to see him as a father figure, which makes Sassoon's return to war a personal loss for both.

questions.stem: How was shell shock often viewed during the First World War?
options: As weakness or cowardice rather than a real injury caused by war
As a serious physical wound treated with surgery at the front
As a condition of the lower ranks, which officers did not usually suffer
As an expected response that the army treated with patience
questions.explanation: Many saw breakdown as a failure of manliness. Rivers argues that it is a natural response to prolonged terror, which challenges the period's ideas about courage.

questions.stem: Which statement about the characters in Regeneration is correct?
options: All the characters are invented, but the hospital and the war are real
All the characters were real people, including Prior, Sarah and Burns
Rivers and Prior were real; Sassoon, Owen and Graves are invented
Sassoon, Owen, Graves, Rivers and Yealland were real; Prior, Sarah and Burns are invented
questions.explanation: Barker mixes real people with fictional ones. The invented characters let her explore class, the home front and trauma beyond what the historical record shows.

questions.stem: Where does the novel's title come from?
options: An Owen poem about spring returning to the battlefields of France
Rivers's real experiments on nerve regeneration, used as a metaphor for healing minds
Rivers's belief that the soldiers' faith in the war must be regenerated
A poem by Sassoon written at Craiglockhart and published in the hospital magazine
questions.explanation: Rivers had studied how cut nerves regrow, in experiments with Henry Head. The title suggests that minds might heal as slowly and painfully as nerves, and asks what they are healed for.

questions.stem: Why might it matter that Barker wrote Regeneration in 1991, long after the war?
options: She drew on her grandfather's war diaries, which make up most of the novel
She could explore subjects the war generation rarely discussed openly, such as trauma and class
She wanted to retell the war as a story of heroism for a new generation
She was responding to the Gulf War, and the novel argues against it directly
questions.explanation: Writing decades later, Barker brings modern understanding of trauma, gender and class to the material. She has said she was interested in the parts of war left out of official accounts.

questions.stem: Which theme is most central to Regeneration?
options: The psychological damage of war and the cost of 'curing' men to fight again
The glory of battle and the honour of dying bravely for one's own country
The importance of strict military discipline in winning a long and difficult war
The romance between soldiers and women on the home front
questions.explanation: The novel focuses on the mental wounds of war. Its central paradox is that healing patients means returning them to the danger that broke them.

questions.stem: How does the novel connect masculinity with breakdown?
options: Men taught to hide fear and feeling break down when forced to suppress them
Men who show their feelings openly are the ones who break down in battle
Men break down because of physical weakness of the nerves, not repressed feeling
Men break down because they lack the will to keep on fighting
questions.explanation: The ideal of the stoic soldier demands silence about fear. Rivers believes his patients' symptoms come partly from that repression, so talking about feelings becomes part of the cure.

questions.stem: How does the novel explore silence and speech?
options: Rivers forbids patients to speak of the war so that they can recover
Patients lose their voices, and Sassoon's protest is silenced by being called illness
Patients talk constantly of battle, and Rivers urges them to forget it
Sassoon is silenced, while the other patients speak about the war freely
questions.explanation: Prior and Callan are mute, and Yealland forces speech with pain. Even Sassoon's declaration is muted by the diagnosis, so the novel asks who is allowed to speak about the war. Rivers encourages men to face their memories rather than forget them.

questions.stem: What does the novel suggest about society's attitude to love between men in wartime?
options: It tolerates homosexuality among soldiers at the front but punishes it severely at home
It discourages friendship between soldiers so that they fight better
It treats close bonds between soldiers as a symptom of shell shock
It encourages deep loyalty between soldiers but fears and punishes homosexuality
questions.explanation: Rivers notes the contradiction: soldiers are meant to love one another, but not too much. The pressure this places on Sassoon and Owen is part of the novel's picture of repression.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the novel's narrative point of view?
options: First person, narrated entirely by Sassoon in a private diary kept at Craiglockhart
First person, narrated by Rivers looking back on 1917 from old age
Third person, limited to Rivers's point of view throughout
Third person, mostly through Rivers, but also through Prior, Sassoon and Sarah
questions.explanation: Moving between viewpoints lets Barker show the hospital from the doctor's side and the patients' side, and take us beyond it to the home front.

questions.stem: Why does Barker include the scene with Yealland and Callan near the end?
options: To contrast Yealland's brutal methods with Rivers's, while showing both aim to return men to war
To show that Yealland's methods are fundamentally different in purpose from Rivers's
To present Yealland as the villain, in clear contrast to the heroic Rivers
To show how officers were treated, as opposed to private soldiers
questions.explanation: The contrast seems to favour Rivers, but the two doctors share a goal. The scene forces Rivers, and readers, to question how different his work really is. Callan is a private, not an officer.

questions.stem: What is the effect of the chapters set outside Craiglockhart with Sarah Lumb?
options: They show the comfortable lives of officers' families in Edinburgh
They offer a romantic escape that has little link to the war
They show the war's effect on the home front and on working-class women
They show what daily life is like for soldiers fighting on the Western Front
questions.explanation: Through Sarah, Barker widens the novel beyond the hospital. Women's war work brings new money and freedom, but also danger.

questions.stem: How does Barker mostly reveal the patients' war experiences?
options: Through conversations, memories and therapy sessions, not battle scenes
Through long, vivid battle scenes set on the Western Front as they happen
Through newspaper reports of battles that the patients read aloud
Through official army records that Rivers reads at his desk
questions.explanation: The fighting reaches us second-hand, through what men can bear to say. This keeps the focus on trauma and memory rather than action.

questions.stem: The novel opens with Sassoon's statement, which he calls 'an act of wilful defiance of military authority'. What is the effect of starting with it?
options: It places a real protest at the centre and raises the question of whether dissent is madness
It shows that Sassoon has already been cured and is ready to return to his battalion
It establishes from the start that Sassoon's protest is a symptom of shell shock
It shows that Sassoon's protest was widely supported in Britain in 1917
questions.explanation: The declaration is Sassoon's real 1917 statement. Opening with it makes readers judge it for themselves before the army calls it a symptom.

questions.stem: Why is the ending, in which Sassoon is passed fit and returns to duty, often read as uneasy?
options: Sassoon has finally agreed that his protest was wrong and that the war is just
Sassoon returns to the front and is killed in action soon after
Sassoon is sent back as a punishment after refusing Rivers's treatment
Rivers's success in his job means sending a man he cares for back into danger
questions.explanation: Rivers has achieved what the army wanted, but at a cost he now feels. The novel closes on his sense of how much his encounter with Sassoon has changed him.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'In Regeneration, healing is not the same as recovery.' Discuss.
options: Barker suggests that Rivers's cures restore men to the army rather than to themselves
In Regeneration, Dr Rivers treats a number of patients at Craiglockhart War Hospital
This essay will discuss healing and recovery in the novel Regeneration by Pat Barker
Regeneration is a novel about the First World War that was published in 1991
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and names what the paragraph will prove. The others retell, announce or state facts without an argument.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'Yealland gives Callan electric shocks until he speaks.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Add the name of the London hospital and the exact date on which the treatment happened
List the other treatments for shell shock that were used during the war
Describe what Callan does after the treatment, one step at a time
Explain how the scene makes Rivers question whether his own methods also silence men
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the evidence suggests. Linking the scene to Rivers's doubts turns a shocking detail into evidence for an argument.
